parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a member of the platform's airspace desk. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through an ordinary working day, from the time you start your shift to when you log off?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace by managing the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. My work deals with planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once, which are often amended during the day.
What is the very first thing you do when you sit down at your desk to start your shift?
I don't know.
Who usually hands work to you, and in what format does it reach you?
I don't know.
Think back to the worst day you've had at work over the last few months—what happened?
I don't know.
Is there anything in your daily work that you currently check by hand because you don't trust the system or the data?
I don't know.
What are you most afraid a new software service would get wrong?
I don't know.
When something goes wrong with a closure or in the airspace, what information do you need to know immediately?

When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. I also deal with closures that can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and closures that are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.
Once you determine the disruption a closure causes, who do you hand that information to?
I don't know.
When an authority suddenly amends a closure while drones are already in the air, what does that look like in practice?

I deal with sudden closures that apply at once, as well as planned ones with a start and end time, and they are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
